jokes.label: Joke A
jokes.title: The Long Answer
jokes.joke: I asked my pharmacist if there was anything for talking too much. He said, 'How long has this been going on?' I said, 'Well, there are two schools of thought, but first you need some context about my childhood.' He said, 'I'm going to have to put you on hold.' I was standing right in front of him.

jokes.label: Joke B
jokes.title: Pharmacist Triage
jokes.joke: My pharmacist looked at my prescription and said, “Take one a day, and don’t mix it with alcohol.” I said, “I came in here to be saved.” She said, “Sir, there are eleven people behind you, and one of them is coughing on the Tylenol display. I can’t save everyone.” So I’m now a statistic on a clipboard, and she’s already moved on to the cough.”

jokes.label: Joke C
jokes.title: Triage at the Register
jokes.joke: I could never be a pharmacist, because I'd struggle with the reality that you just can't save everyone. When a guy comes to the counter at midnight buying generic Viagra, Axe body spray, and a single Red Bull... legally, I have to just bag it up. But out of pure compassion? I want to grab his hand, look him in the eye, and whisper, 'Bro... she's not coming over.'

jokes.label: Joke D
jokes.title: Pharmacy TED Talk
jokes.joke: My pharmacist is ridiculously verbose. I asked for something for a headache and he launched into a full lecture on ibuprofen's molecular structure, half-life, and seventeen possible interactions. By the time he finished, the headache had upgraded itself to a migraine just to drown him out.

jokes.label: Joke E
jokes.title: Side Effects Lecture
jokes.joke: I knew my pharmacist was a little too talkative when I picked up a prescription and he said, "Any questions?" Thirty minutes later, I was the one asking if there’d be a quiz. The label said, "Take once daily," but somehow the verbal instructions included character development, a sequel, and director’s commentary.

scores.comment: The setup feels forced, and the final clipboard-and-cough line is confusing rather than funny. The premise explicitly incorporates both seeds but lacks a satisfying comic turn.

Strong, recognizable comic situation with specific visual details and a punchline that reframes the pharmacist's inability to save someone. Slightly overexplained setup, but the final line delivers a genuine laugh.
Clear and economical, but the talkative person making a headache worse is an obvious premise. The migraine punchline largely restates the setup, with little surprise.
Natural first-person delivery with amusing exaggeration and decent escalation. The quiz line is familiar, and the final list provides comic imagery without a particularly sharp concluding punch.
The comic proves the diagnosis by being verbose in the middle of the bit, and the closing line is a decent absurd snap. The ‘on hold’ turn is slightly muddled but lands.
A concrete, recognizable image (Viagra, Axe, a lone Red Bull) builds to a clear, funny final line. The ‘can’t save everyone’ concept is reframed neatly as misplaced compassion.
The idea of a headache upgrading itself to a migraine to drown him out is a pleasant twist. The setup tells us he is ‘verbose’ instead of showing it, and the premise is familiar.
The ‘will there be a quiz’ beat is mildly funny. The closing list of movie-extras comparisons (sequel, director’s commentary) is predictable and reads as a stack of similar jokes.

Excellent stage premise with a very strong, visual punchline ('put you on hold' in person). The execution is tight and the demonstration of the 'verbose' seed term through dialogue rather than exposition is top-notch.
The setup feels unnatural; asking to be 'saved' when told not to mix meds with alcohol doesn't flow logically. The punchline just restates the seed term rather than finding a clever angle on it.
Competent but very predictable. The 'pharmacist explains molecules' trope is a standard exaggeration, and the punchline about the headache upgrading is a familiar comedy shape.
A solid, well-crafted joke. It takes the same basic premise as Joke D but executes it much better with a sharp rule of three at the end ('character development, a sequel, and director's commentary').
Clean in-person hold callback after verbose setup; solid timing but familiar customer-service shape.
On-the-nose restatement of the seed; final clipboard image is flat and fails to snap.
Specific midnight purchase list builds a clear loser image; compassion whisper lands cleanly as the turn.
Quiz beat is mild filler; movie-metaphor extension is serviceable but over-extended.
Solid misdirection and strong final tag; familiar talkative-person premise limits freshness.
Concept is clear, but the escalation feels forced and the ending lands softly.
Strong premise, specific image, and a clean reveal that pays off with a relatable human observation.
Competent and clear, but the headache-becomes-a-migraine punchline is a very familiar route.
